questions.q: An investment falls by {f}. What percentage gain does it need to get back to where it started? (Nearest whole %.)
questions.why: After a {f} fall you have (1 − {f}) left; you need {answer}% on that to recover. Losses hurt more than equal gains help.

questions.q: Why is diversification called the "free lunch" of investing?
options: It cuts risk without cutting expected return
It guarantees you won't lose money
questions.why: Company risk largely cancels out across many holdings, and investors aren't paid for taking it, so removing it costs nothing in expected return.

questions.q: Match each event to the kind of risk it is.
questions.why: Company risk hits one firm and can be diversified away; market risk hits nearly everything.

questions.q: Two investments have a correlation of 1. What does spreading money between them do to risk?
questions.why: With correlation 1 they always move together, so combining them doesn't smooth anything. Lower correlation means more benefit.

questions.q: Investors are paid a higher expected return for holding one company's shares instead of a fund of many similar companies.
questions.why: Company risk can be removed cheaply by diversifying, so the market doesn't reward it. One share is riskier for the same expected return.

questions.q: What is the equity risk premium?
options: The extra expected return from shares over safe assets, as payment for their risk
questions.why: It's the reward investors demand for living with the swings of shares rather than holding cash.

questions.q: Put these goals in order, from the one that suits the least risk to the one that can take the most.
items: Saving for a child's university in 12 years
questions.why: The longer until you need the money, the more time to recover from falls, so the more risk you can usually afford.

options: How much a price swings up and down
questions.why: Volatility is the size of the swings. Higher volatility means a wider range of possible results.

questions.q: Big falls in share markets, like about half in 2008, are rare one-offs that long-term investors are unlikely to see again.
questions.why: Big falls happen regularly: 2008, the 2020 Covid crash and others. Long-term investors should expect to live through several.

questions.q: Explain why holding 500 companies is less risky than holding one, without lowering the expected return.

ideas.label: One company's bad luck is cancelled out by others doing well (company risk cancels)
The market doesn't pay extra for company risk, so expected return stays about the same

questions.model: With 500 companies, one company's bad news is balanced by others doing well, so company risk largely cancels out. Because anyone can remove that risk this way, the market doesn't pay extra for taking it, so the expected return of the 500 is about the same as one similar company, with far less risk.
questions.why: Diversification removes the risk you're not paid for.

tests.answer: Bad news at one company is cancelled out by the others, and you aren't paid extra for company risk so the expected return stays the same.
Because the risk is spread out.

questions.q: Explain why someone who would panic and sell after a 30% fall is taking too much risk, even if they're investing for 30 years.

ideas.label: Selling after a fall locks in the loss (turns a temporary fall into a permanent one)
Risk must match how you'll actually behave, not just the timeframe

questions.model: Selling after a fall turns a temporary drop into a permanent loss and means missing the recovery. A long timeframe only helps if you stay invested, so the right level of risk depends on how you'll actually behave in a crash, not just how long you're investing for.
questions.why: Behaviour turns volatility into real losses.

tests.answer: Selling locks in the loss and they miss the recovery, so risk has to match how they will actually behave.
They would lose money by selling at the bottom.
